explain.text:
Now with the full figure visible, the three panels line up clearly with the text's description.

Left (plain networks): olive=plain-20, cyan=plain-32, green=plain-44, red=plain-56. Dotted lines are training error, bold are test error. Before the rate drop at iteration ~3.3×10⁴, red (56-layer) is actually bouncing around the highest error, briefly pinned at the 20% ceiling. After the drop, the deeper nets settle worse: 56-layer holds around 12-13% test error, clearly above the 20-layer line near 10%. Deeper plain net = worse result, both train and test — the degradation problem.

Middle (ResNets): same color code plus black=ResNet-110. Before the drop, curves are tangled together, bouncing between 10-20%. After it, everything collapses to a tight band near 6-9%, and the labelled "110-layer" line sits at the bottom of that band, while "20-layer" sits at the top. So here more depth means lower error — the opposite ordering from the plain case.

Right (extreme depth): black=residual-110 sits around 6.5-7%, magenta=residual-1202 sits a bit higher, around 7.5-8%, both commented in the text as training smoothly with the test gap chalked up to overfitting on the small dataset rather than optimization failure.

ask.text: The 1202-layer curve (residual-1202) is magenta, and it settles at roughly 7.5-8% test error, running consistently just above the black 110-layer curve, which sits closer to 6.5-7%. That matches the text's reported figures — 7.93% for the 1202-layer net versus 6.43% for the 110-layer one — with the gap attributed to overfitting on CIFAR-10's small dataset rather than any optimization difficulty, since the dotted training-error lines for both are near 0 and essentially overlapping.
